# (PART) Foundations {#sec-part-foundations .unnumbered}

# Introduction to Research Synthesis {#sec-introduction}

A single study rarely settles a question. Samples are finite, measures are imperfect, and every
study is run in one place, at one time, with one population and one version of the intervention.
When a literature contains dozens or hundreds of studies of the same question, the useful
question is no longer "what did this study find?" but "what does the body of evidence say, how
certain is it, and how much do the results vary across settings?" Research synthesis is the
collection of methods that answer that question in a transparent and reproducible way, and
meta-analysis is its statistical core.

This chapter sets up the rest of the book. It explains why evidence needs to be synthesized
formally, sketches how the field developed, distinguishes narrative reviews, systematic reviews,
and meta-analyses, and defines what a meta-analysis actually estimates. A small simulation shows
why counting significant results is a poor substitute for pooling estimates, and a second one
shows why meta-analyses of a single paper's studies deserve caution. The chapter closes with the
limits of the method, a tour of the R ecosystem, a complete first analysis, and a roadmap.

## Why synthesize evidence {#sec-introduction-why}

There are three reasons to combine studies rather than read them one at a time. The first is
precision. Individual studies in psychology, management, marketing, and much of clinical
medicine are small relative to the effects they try to detect, so their estimates are noisy and
their significance tests have low power. Pooling the information in many studies gives an
estimate whose standard error shrinks roughly with the square root of the total sample size.

The second reason is generalization. Studies differ in populations, settings, dosages, measures,
and designs. A synthesis can ask whether an effect holds across that variation, how much it
varies, and which study features are associated with larger or smaller effects. A single study,
however large, says little about the population of settings in which an intervention might be
used.

The third reason is protection against bias in how evidence is read. Informal summaries tend to
overweight vivid, recent, famous, or congenial studies. A synthesis that specifies its question,
search, inclusion criteria, and analysis in advance, and reports each step, makes these choices
visible and open to criticism [@cooper2019handbook; @gurevitch2018meta]. It also makes the
synthesis updatable: when new studies appear, the analysis can be rerun rather than rewritten.

## A short history {#sec-introduction-history}

The idea of combining results is older than the name. In 1904 Karl Pearson collected data from
several samples of British soldiers on typhoid (enteric fever) inoculation, computed the
correlation between inoculation and both infection and mortality in each sample, and averaged
them [@pearson1904report]. The correlations were modest and irregular across samples, and
Pearson called for more carefully designed investigation before the procedure was adopted
routinely. Combining independent estimates had a longer history still in astronomy, and in the
1930s statisticians working on agricultural experiments developed methods for combining the
results of several trials [@chalmers2002brief].

The modern field took shape in the 1970s. @light1971accumulating examined how reviewers resolve
contradictory study results and criticized the habit of tallying significant and non-significant
findings. Gene Glass introduced the term *meta-analysis* in his 1976 presidential address to the
American Educational Research Association, defining it as the statistical analysis of a large
collection of results from individual studies for the purpose of integrating the findings
[@glass1976primary]. @smith1977meta applied the idea to several hundred controlled evaluations of
psychotherapy and concluded that psychotherapy was, on average, effective. The response was
sharp: @eysenck1978exercise dismissed the exercise as "mega-silliness", arguing that pooling
studies of mixed quality and different therapies produced a meaningless average. Two of the
standard criticisms of meta-analysis, "garbage in, garbage out" and "apples and oranges", date
from this exchange and are discussed in Section \@ref(sec-introduction-limits).

Statistical foundations followed quickly. @rosenthal1979file formalized the "file drawer
problem", the worry that non-significant studies remain unpublished. @hedges1980vote showed that
vote counting can become *less* likely to detect a true effect as studies accumulate, and
@hedges1985statistical laid out the theory of effect sizes, their sampling distributions,
weighted estimation, and tests of homogeneity that underlies nearly every method in this book.
In medicine, the push to base clinical practice on systematic summaries of randomized trials led
to the founding of the Cochrane Collaboration in 1993, named after the epidemiologist Archie
Cochrane, with the aim of preparing, maintaining, and disseminating systematic reviews of the
effects of health care [@chalmers1993cochrane]. The Campbell Collaboration followed for social
policy, education, and crime. Today meta-analysis is used across the sciences, from ecology to
economics [@gurevitch2018meta], and its volume has grown so fast that redundant and conflicted
meta-analyses have become a problem in their own right [@ioannidis2016mass].

## Narrative reviews, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses {#sec-introduction-review-types}

Three terms are often used interchangeably but mean different things.

A **narrative review** summarizes a literature in prose, usually written by an expert who
selects and interprets the studies. Narrative reviews are valuable for framing a field, tracing
the development of ideas, and building theory. Their weakness is that the search, selection, and
weighting of studies are implicit. Two experts can read the same literature and reach opposite
conclusions without either being able to point to where their methods diverged.

A **systematic review** answers a pre-specified question using explicit, reproducible methods: a
protocol, a documented search of multiple sources, eligibility criteria applied in duplicate,
structured data extraction, and an assessment of risk of bias in each included study
[@higgins2019cochrane]. A systematic review need not contain any statistics. When studies are too
different to combine, the synthesis may be structured narratively, for example by grouping
studies and tabulating their results. Chapter \@ref(sec-systematic-review) covers this workflow
in detail.

A **meta-analysis** is the statistical combination of results from two or more studies. It is
usually, and ideally, embedded in a systematic review, since a pooled estimate is only as
trustworthy as the process that selected the studies feeding it. Meta-analytic methods are also
applied outside systematic reviews, for example to combine the studies in a multi-study paper
(Section \@ref(sec-introduction-internal)) or the sites of a multi-lab replication. Throughout
the book, "meta-analysis" refers to the statistical component and "systematic review" to the
surrounding process.

## What a meta-analysis estimates {#sec-introduction-estimands}

Suppose there are $k$ studies, and study $i$ reports an effect size estimate $y_i$ (a log risk
ratio, a standardized mean difference, a Fisher-$z$ correlation) with sampling variance $v_i$,
treated as known. Chapter \@ref(sec-effect-sizes) shows how to compute $y_i$ and $v_i$ from the
statistics that studies report. What the meta-analysis estimates depends on the model one is
willing to assume for the true effects $\theta_i$ that the studies estimate.

In the **common-effect** (also called fixed-effect or equal-effects) model all studies estimate
the same quantity:

$$
y_i = \theta + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, v_i).
$$

The target is the single parameter $\theta$, estimated by the inverse-variance weighted mean
$\hat\theta = \sum_i w_i y_i / \sum_i w_i$ with $w_i = 1/v_i$ and
$\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta) = (\sum_i w_i)^{-1/2}$.

In the **random-effects** model the true effects themselves vary across studies, because
populations, interventions, and measures differ:

$$
y_i = \mu + u_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad u_i \sim N(0, \tau^2), \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, v_i).
$$

There are now two targets: the mean $\mu$ of the distribution of true effects and its standard
deviation $\tau$. The mean alone answers "what is the effect on average across settings like
these?", but it does not say what to expect in a new setting. For that the relevant summary is
the **prediction interval**, which under normality is approximately
$\hat\mu \pm t_{k-2,\,0.975}\sqrt{\hat\tau^2 + \operatorname{SE}(\hat\mu)^2}$
[@higgins2009reevaluation; @riley2011interpretation]. When heterogeneity is substantial, the
confidence interval for $\mu$ can exclude zero while the prediction interval comfortably includes
it.

The choice between these models is a choice of estimand, not only of method. Under the
common-effect model the question is whether "the" effect exists and how big it is. Under the
random-effects model the question is about a distribution: its center, its spread, and the
proportion of settings in which the effect is beneficial or harmful
[@borenstein2010basic]. A third reading, sometimes called the fixed-effects (plural) model,
treats the $\theta_i$ as fixed but different and interprets the weighted mean as the average
effect in the particular set of studies at hand, without any claim about other settings
[@rice2017reevaluation]. Chapter \@ref(sec-models) develops these models formally, compares
estimators of $\tau^2$, and discusses inference with few studies.

## Why vote counting fails {#sec-introduction-vote-counting}

Before meta-analysis, a common way to summarize a literature was to count how many studies found
a significant effect and declare the effect "established" if most did. This is called **vote
counting**. It fails for a simple reason: whether a study reaches significance depends on its
power as much as on the size of the effect. When the typical study is underpowered, most studies
will be non-significant even when the effect is real, and a vote count will conclude that the
evidence is mixed or negative [@light1971accumulating; @hedges1980vote].

A small simulation makes this concrete. Consider twenty two-group studies with 30 participants
per group, all estimating the same true standardized mean difference of $\delta = 0.3$, a
modest effect of the size common in the behavioral sciences.

```{r intro-vote-sim}
set.seed(1904)
k <- 20; n <- 30; delta <- 0.3

# simulate raw data for one two-group study and keep the summary statistics
sim_study <- function(n, delta) {
  x1 <- rnorm(n, mean = delta, sd = 1)
  x2 <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  c(m1 = mean(x1), m2 = mean(x2), sd1 = sd(x1), sd2 = sd(x2),
    p = t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value)
}
studies <- as.data.frame(t(replicate(k, sim_study(n, delta))))
studies$n1 <- n; studies$n2 <- n

# vote count
n_sig <- sum(studies$p < 0.05)
n_sig

# meta-analysis of the same studies (Hedges' g, common-effect model)
dat_sim <- escalc(measure = "SMD", m1i = m1, m2i = m2, sd1i = sd1, sd2i = sd2,
                  n1i = n1, n2i = n2, data = studies)
fit_sim <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat_sim, method = "EE")
fit_sim
```

```{r intro-vote-numbers, include = FALSE}
pw <- power.t.test(n = n, delta = delta, sd = 1)$power
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
fp <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< .001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", p))
```

Only `r n_sig` of the `r k` studies are significant at the 5% level, so a vote count would
conclude that the effect does not replicate. Yet the pooled estimate is
$\hat\theta = `r f2(coef(fit_sim))`$ with 95% CI
[`r f2(fit_sim$ci.lb)`, `r f2(fit_sim$ci.ub)`] and $p$ `r fp(fit_sim$pval)`.
The data are perfectly consistent with a single true effect (the $Q$ test gives
$p$ = `r round(fit_sim$QEp, 2)`), and the confidence interval covers the true value of 0.3. The
studies do not disagree; they are simply too small to detect the effect one at a time. The power
of each study here is only `r round(pw, 2)`.

The problem gets worse, not better, as evidence accumulates. Suppose a reviewer declares an effect
established if more than half of $k$ studies are significant. If each study has power $\pi$, the
number of significant studies is binomial, and the probability that the vote count finds the
effect is $P(\text{Bin}(k, \pi) > k/2)$. When $\pi < 0.5$ this probability goes to zero as $k$
grows. The power of the pooled test, in contrast, goes to one, since the standard error of the
pooled estimate shrinks as $1/\sqrt{k}$. Figure \@ref(fig:intro-vote-plot) shows both curves for
the design above.

```{r intro-vote-plot, fig.cap = "Probability of concluding that an effect exists, by number of studies, when every study has 30 participants per group and the true standardized mean difference is 0.3. Vote counting (more than half significant) becomes less likely to detect the effect as studies accumulate; the pooled common-effect test becomes more likely.", fig.height = 4}
ks <- 1:60
se_pooled <- sqrt((2 / n + delta^2 / (4 * n)) / ks)   # approximate SE of pooled d
curves <- data.frame(
  k = rep(ks, 2),
  prob = c(1 - pbinom(floor(ks / 2), ks, pw),
           pnorm(delta / se_pooled - qnorm(0.975))),
  method = rep(c("Vote count (majority significant)", "Meta-analysis (pooled z-test)"),
               each = length(ks))
)
ggplot(curves, aes(k, prob, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Number of studies (k)", y = "Probability of detecting the effect",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The lesson generalizes beyond this example. Counting significant results discards the
information in the effect estimates and their precision, confuses "not significant" with "no
effect", and is biased toward the null when studies are small. If studies report too little to
compute effect sizes, better options exist than vote counting on significance: Chapter
\@ref(sec-effect-sizes) shows how to recover effect sizes from test statistics and $p$-values,
and the Cochrane Handbook describes structured alternatives when even that is impossible
[@higgins2019cochrane].

## Internal meta-analyses and p-hacking {#sec-introduction-internal}

Multi-study papers in psychology, consumer research, and management increasingly end with a
meta-analysis of their own studies, sometimes called an *internal* or *single-paper*
meta-analysis. The appeal is real: individual studies may be small and inconclusive, and a
pooled estimate summarizes the paper's evidence and supports cumulative science
[@mcshane2017single]. The danger is that a pooled analysis of a small set of studies chosen and
analyzed by the same authors inherits, and amplifies, every undisclosed choice made along the
way.

Two assumptions are needed for an internal meta-analysis to be trustworthy
[@Vosgerau_2019]. First, none of the individual studies may be even slightly $p$-hacked, for
example by choosing among dependent variables, covariates, or exclusion rules after seeing the
data [@Simmons_2011]. Because the same lab tends to make the same choices in every study, small
biases do not average out across studies; they accumulate. Second, the set of studies must be
complete: the authors must not have left out studies that "did not work", or run additional
studies until the pooled result became significant [@ueno2016meta]. A file drawer of one or two
studies per paper is enough to distort a five-study internal meta-analysis.

The following simulation, in the spirit of @Vosgerau_2019, shows how fast the false-positive
rate grows. The true effect is zero. Each of five studies has 40 participants per group and
measures three outcomes that correlate at 0.5. In the honest scenario the authors report the
pre-specified first outcome. In the hacked scenario they report whichever outcome shows the
largest effect, which is a mild form of selective reporting. A third scenario runs eight studies
honestly but reports the five with the largest estimates. Estimates are drawn from their
large-sample normal distribution, $d \sim N(0, 2/n)$, which is adequate here.

```{r intro-internal-sim}
set.seed(2019)
nsim <- 4000; n <- 40; m <- 3; rho <- 0.5
se_d <- sqrt(2 / n)
R <- matrix(rho, m, m); diag(R) <- 1
U <- chol(R)

# nsim x nstud x m array of estimated effects under the null
draw <- function(nstud) {
  z <- matrix(rnorm(nsim * nstud * m), ncol = m) %*% U * se_d
  array(z, c(nsim, nstud, m))
}
# two-sided p-value of a common-effect meta-analysis with equal variances
pool_p <- function(est) {
  z <- rowMeans(est) / (se_d / sqrt(ncol(est)))
  2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
}

d5 <- draw(5)
honest <- d5[, , 1]                     # pre-specified outcome
hacked <- apply(d5, c(1, 2), max)       # best of three outcomes
d8 <- draw(8)[, , 1]
dropped <- t(apply(d8, 1, function(x) sort(x, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]))

fpr <- c(
  study_honest   = mean(2 * pnorm(-abs(honest / se_d)) < 0.05),
  study_hacked   = mean(2 * pnorm(-abs(hacked / se_d)) < 0.05),
  meta_honest    = mean(pool_p(honest) < 0.05),
  meta_hacked    = mean(pool_p(hacked) < 0.05),
  meta_5_of_8    = mean(pool_p(dropped) < 0.05)
)
round(fpr, 3)
```

At the level of a single study, choosing the best of three correlated outcomes barely moves the
two-sided false-positive rate, from `r round(fpr["study_honest"], 3)` to
`r round(fpr["study_hacked"], 3)`. That looks harmless. In the internal meta-analysis the same
habit raises the false-positive rate from `r round(fpr["meta_honest"], 3)` to
`r round(fpr["meta_hacked"], 3)`, because the small upward bias is repeated in every study while
the standard error of the pooled estimate shrinks. Quietly reporting five of eight null studies
gives a false-positive rate of `r round(fpr["meta_5_of_8"], 3)`. The more studies a paper
pools, the more precisely it estimates its own bias.

::: {.rmdwarning}
An internal meta-analysis is informative only if every study is reported, each was analyzed as
pre-registered, and the decision to stop collecting studies did not depend on the results. When
these conditions cannot be verified, treat a significant pooled estimate from a single paper as
a summary of that paper's evidence, not as independent confirmation. Pre-registration of each
study and of the pooling plan is the most direct safeguard [@Vosgerau_2019; @mcshane2017single].
:::

The same logic applies to meta-analyses of published literatures, where selective publication
and selective reporting play the role of the file drawer. Chapter \@ref(sec-publication-bias)
treats methods to detect and adjust for these biases, including $p$-curve
[@simonsohn2014p], selection models, and regression-based corrections.

## Limits of meta-analysis {#sec-introduction-limits}

Meta-analysis is a tool for combining evidence, not for creating it. Three classic criticisms
remain relevant, and each has a methodological answer that the later chapters develop
[@sharpe1997apples].

**Garbage in, garbage out.** Pooling biased studies yields a precise estimate of a biased
quantity. Precision is not validity. Eysenck's objection applies with full force to any
meta-analysis that includes studies without assessing their risk of bias. The answer is not to
exclude all imperfect studies by fiat, but to assess risk of bias with validated tools, examine
whether effects differ by risk of bias, and grade the certainty of the pooled evidence
accordingly (Chapters \@ref(sec-systematic-review) and \@ref(sec-reporting)).

**Apples and oranges.** Studies that differ in population, intervention, comparator, and outcome
may not estimate the same thing. Whether combining them is sensible depends on the question:
"fruit" is a legitimate category for some purposes and not for others. Random-effects models make
the heterogeneity explicit rather than assuming it away, and subgroup analysis and
meta-regression ask whether study characteristics explain it (Chapters \@ref(sec-models) and
\@ref(sec-heterogeneity)). A large $\tau$ with a wide prediction interval is itself a finding: the
average effect is a poor guide to what will happen in any particular setting.

**The file drawer.** If studies with significant or favorable results are more likely to be
published, found, or fully reported, the studies available to a meta-analysis are a biased
sample [@rosenthal1979file]. Comprehensive searching, including trial registries and grey
literature (Chapter \@ref(sec-systematic-review)), reduces the problem; small-study and
selection-model methods (Chapter \@ref(sec-publication-bias)) can diagnose and partly correct it,
but no statistical method fully recovers studies that were never seen.

Two further limits deserve mention. Associations between study characteristics and effect sizes
are observational, even when every included study is a randomized trial, because studies were
not randomized to their characteristics. And meta-analyses can be numerous, overlapping, and
conflicted: many topics have several published meta-analyses with different inclusion criteria
and conclusions [@ioannidis2016mass]. Transparent protocols, open data, and reproducible code
are the best defense, and they are a theme throughout the book.

## The R ecosystem for meta-analysis {#sec-introduction-r}

R has the most complete set of meta-analysis tools of any statistical environment. The CRAN Task
View on meta-analysis (<https://CRAN.R-project.org/view=MetaAnalysis>) lists well over a hundred
packages. Table \@ref(tab:intro-packages) lists the ones used most in this book.

```{r intro-packages, echo = FALSE}
pkgs <- data.frame(
  Package = c("metafor", "meta", "metadat", "clubSandwich", "netmeta",
              "metaSEM", "brms", "bayesmeta", "robvis", "PRISMA2020"),
  Purpose = c(
    "General framework: effect sizes, common/random-effects and multilevel models, meta-regression, diagnostics, plots",
    "Convenient interfaces for standard pairwise analyses and publication-ready forest plots",
    "About a hundred published meta-analytic datasets used as examples throughout",
    "Cluster-robust variance estimation with small-sample corrections for dependent effects",
    "Frequentist network meta-analysis",
    "Meta-analytic structural equation modeling",
    "Bayesian multilevel models via Stan, including meta-analytic models",
    "Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis with exact posterior computation",
    "Risk-of-bias summary and traffic-light plots",
    "PRISMA 2020 flow diagrams"
  )
)
knitr::kable(pkgs, caption = "Core R packages used in this book.")
```

The workhorse is **metafor** [@viechtbauer2010conducting], which implements effect size
computation (`escalc()`), common-effect, random-effects, and mixed-effects models (`rma()`),
multilevel and multivariate models (`rma.mv()`), and a large set of diagnostics and plots. The
**meta** package offers a higher-level interface that many applied researchers find convenient
[@balduzzi2019how]. Datasets come from **metadat**, which is loaded automatically with metafor.
Dependent effect sizes are handled with **clubSandwich** [@pustejovsky2017small], network
meta-analysis with **netmeta** [@balduzzi2023netmeta], meta-analytic structural equation models
with **metaSEM** [@cheung2015metasem], and Bayesian models with **brms** [@burkner2017brms] and
**bayesmeta** [@rover2020bayesian]. Each chapter loads the packages it needs explicitly.

## A first meta-analysis in R {#sec-introduction-quickstart}

This section runs a complete meta-analysis in four steps, so that the vocabulary of later
chapters has something concrete to attach to. Each step is explained briefly and revisited in
depth later.

The data are 13 trials of the Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine against tuberculosis
[@colditz1994efficacy], available as `dat.bcg` in metadat. For each trial we have the number of
tuberculosis cases and non-cases in the vaccinated and control groups.

```{r intro-bcg-data}
head(dat.bcg, 4)
```

### Step 1: compute effect sizes {#sec-introduction-qs-escalc}

The natural effect size for a binary outcome in a trial is the risk ratio. Meta-analysis works on
the log scale, where the sampling distribution is closer to normal and the variance has a simple
form. `escalc()` adds the log risk ratio `yi` and its sampling variance `vi` to the data.

```{r intro-bcg-escalc}
dat <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,
              data = dat.bcg, slab = paste(author, year))
dat[1:4, c("author", "year", "yi", "vi")]
```

The first trial has $y_1$ = `r round(dat$yi[1], 3)`, a risk ratio of
`r round(exp(dat$yi[1]), 2)`: vaccinated participants had about `r round(100 * (1 - exp(dat$yi[1])))`%
lower risk of tuberculosis than controls. Chapter \@ref(sec-effect-sizes) covers effect sizes for
binary, continuous, and correlational data and their variances.

### Step 2: fit a random-effects model {#sec-introduction-qs-rma}

The trials were run in very different places, from the southern United States to Northern
Europe, so a common true effect is implausible. `rma()` fits a random-effects model, estimating
$\tau^2$ by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) by default.

```{r intro-bcg-rma}
res <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat)
res
```

The estimated mean log risk ratio is $\hat\mu$ = `r round(coef(res), 3)` (SE =
`r round(res$se, 3)`), clearly different from zero. Heterogeneity is large: $\hat\tau$ =
`r round(sqrt(res$tau2), 3)` on the log scale, $I^2$ = `r round(res$I2, 1)`%, and the $Q$ test
rejects homogeneity ($Q$ = `r round(res$QE, 1)` on `r res$k - 1` degrees of freedom). The
estimate of $\tau$ is the more interpretable of these: it is the standard deviation of true log
risk ratios across settings, on the same scale as the effect. Chapter \@ref(sec-models) discusses
the choice of $\tau^2$ estimator and of confidence-interval method (for example Hartung-Knapp),
and Chapter \@ref(sec-heterogeneity) explains why $I^2$ alone is not a measure of how much
effects vary.

### Step 3: interpret on the risk-ratio scale {#sec-introduction-qs-predict}

`predict()` back-transforms the mean and its intervals to the risk ratio scale and adds the
prediction interval.

```{r intro-bcg-predict}
pred <- predict(res, transf = exp, digits = 2)
pred
```

On average across settings like these, vaccination multiplies the risk of tuberculosis by
`r f2(pred$pred)` (95% CI `r f2(pred$ci.lb)` to `r f2(pred$ci.ub)`), roughly
halving it. The 95% prediction interval, `r f2(pred$pi.lb)` to `r f2(pred$pi.ub)`, is
far wider: in a new setting comparable to these trials, the true effect could plausibly range
from a large reduction in risk to no benefit, or even a modest increase in risk. That spread is the most decision-relevant
feature of this evidence. Chapter \@ref(sec-heterogeneity) shows that much of it is explained by
the absolute latitude of the trial site.

### Step 4: draw a forest plot {#sec-introduction-qs-forest}

The forest plot is the standard display of a meta-analysis: each study's estimate and confidence
interval, with box size proportional to its weight, and the pooled estimate as a diamond at the
bottom (Figure \@ref(fig:intro-bcg-forest)).

```{r intro-bcg-forest, fig.cap = "Forest plot of 13 BCG vaccine trials (risk ratios, log scale) with the random-effects summary. The dotted line extending from the summary polygon is the 95\\% prediction interval.", fig.height = 6}
forest(res, atransf = exp, at = log(c(0.05, 0.25, 1, 4)), xlim = c(-10, 6),
       header = c("Trial", "Risk ratio [95% CI]"), addpred = TRUE, cex = 0.8)
```

Several trials favor the vaccine strongly, a few show essentially no effect, and the confidence
intervals of some trials do not overlap. A reader of the forest plot sees both the average
benefit and the heterogeneity that the prediction interval quantifies. A complete analysis would
go further: it would explore moderators (Chapter \@ref(sec-heterogeneity)), check for
small-study effects (Chapter \@ref(sec-publication-bias)), assess the influence of individual
trials (Chapter \@ref(sec-sensitivity)), rate the certainty of the evidence and report it
(Chapter \@ref(sec-reporting)). The same four steps, though, are the skeleton of every analysis
in the book.

## Roadmap of the book {#sec-introduction-roadmap}

The book is organized in four parts.

**Part I, Foundations**, consists of this chapter, the systematic review workflow from question
to risk-of-bias assessment (Chapter \@ref(sec-systematic-review)), and effect sizes and their
conversions (Chapter \@ref(sec-effect-sizes)).

**Part II, Core Methods**, develops the statistical machinery used in nearly every meta-analysis:
common-effect and random-effects models (Chapter \@ref(sec-models)); heterogeneity, subgroup
analysis, and meta-regression (Chapter \@ref(sec-heterogeneity)); dependent effect sizes from the
same study, including multilevel models and robust variance estimation
(Chapter \@ref(sec-dependent-effects)); publication bias and small-study effects
(Chapter \@ref(sec-publication-bias)); and sensitivity analysis and diagnostics
(Chapter \@ref(sec-sensitivity)).

**Part III, Advanced Methods**, extends the framework: Bayesian meta-analysis
(Chapter \@ref(sec-bayesian)), network meta-analysis for comparing several interventions
(Chapter \@ref(sec-network)), meta-analytic structural equation modeling
(Chapter \@ref(sec-masem)), multivariate, dose-response, and individual participant data
meta-analysis (Chapter \@ref(sec-multivariate-ipd)), diagnostic test accuracy
(Chapter \@ref(sec-dta)), and the synthesis of causal estimates from quasi-experimental designs
(Chapter \@ref(sec-causal-estimates)).

**Part IV, Reporting**, covers rating the certainty of evidence with GRADE and reporting to
PRISMA 2020 and related standards (Chapter \@ref(sec-reporting)), and ends with a workflow
checklist (Chapter \@ref(sec-conclusion)).

Readers new to meta-analysis should read Chapters \@ref(sec-systematic-review) to
\@ref(sec-sensitivity) in order. Readers who know the basics can go directly to the chapter
for their problem; each chapter states what it assumes.

## Key takeaways {#sec-introduction-takeaways}

- Research synthesis answers questions that single studies cannot: what the body of evidence
  says, how precisely, and how much effects vary across settings.
- A systematic review is a transparent, reproducible process; a meta-analysis is the statistical
  combination of results, ideally embedded in such a review.
- The common-effect model estimates one parameter; the random-effects model estimates the mean
  and the standard deviation of a distribution of true effects. The prediction interval, not the
  confidence interval, describes what to expect in a new setting.
- Vote counting on statistical significance is biased toward the null when studies are
  underpowered and can become less accurate as studies accumulate. Pool effect estimates instead.
- Internal (single-paper) meta-analyses amplify small, undisclosed analytic choices and selective
  inclusion of studies. They are trustworthy only when every study is reported and analyzed as
  pre-registered.
- Meta-analysis cannot fix biased primary studies, incomparable studies, or missing studies; it
  can make these problems visible and quantify their likely impact.

## Further reading {#sec-introduction-reading}

@borenstein2021introduction is the most accessible full-length introduction to the concepts in
this chapter, and @cooper2019handbook is the standard reference handbook for research synthesis
in the social and behavioral sciences. @higgins2019cochrane is the authoritative guide for
systematic reviews of health interventions. @hedges1985statistical remains the classic statement
of the statistical theory. For history, @chalmers2002brief is short and readable;
@gurevitch2018meta surveys the role of meta-analysis across scientific fields. On internal
meta-analyses, read @Vosgerau_2019 alongside @mcshane2017single for the two sides of the
argument. @viechtbauer2010conducting and @balduzzi2019how are practical introductions to the two
main R packages.
